opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and my honest view is that morphology shouldn't be the first thing a startup optimizes for. It should follow from the task and the data strategy, not the other way around.

There's a temptation right now, especially with all the excitement around humanoids, to start from the form factor because it's the most visible and the most fundraising-friendly. A humanoid on stage is compelling. But if you ask what actually creates value in the near term, it's whether the robot can reliably complete useful tasks in real environments, and whether you can collect enough high-quality data to keep improving it.

So I'd frame the priority like this. First, pick a set of tasks where there's real demand and where you can close the loop: deploy, collect data, retrain, redeploy. Second, choose the simplest embodiment that covers those tasks well. In many cases that's a wheeled base with one or two arms, not legs. Wheels are cheaper, more stable, easier to maintain, and the majority of indoor environments, like factories, warehouses, and even homes, are mostly flat. Legs solve a real problem, but it's often not the problem the customer is paying you to solve today.

Third, and this is where I think the humanoid argument does have merit, think about generalization and data reuse. Human-like arms and hands let you learn from human demonstration data, teleoperation, even video, much more naturally. So for the manipulation part, I'd lean toward something anthropomorphic. The upper body matters more than the lower body for most tasks. Dexterous hands are hard and expensive, but grippers alone will cap what you can do eventually.

The last point is about not overcommitting. Hardware iteration cycles are slow and costly, and the field is moving fast on the model side. If you lock yourself into a very specific, very complex body too early, you can end up spending all your resources on mechanical engineering instead of intelligence. I'd rather a startup keep the hardware modular, treat the body as something that will evolve, and invest the core effort into the models and the data flywheel. Ultimately, the morphology that wins will be the one that lets the brain learn fastest and get deployed most widely, not necessarily the one that looks most like us.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes useful tasks, data collection, and adaptable hardware, but does not identify insufficient intelligence as the primary bottleneck for robotics startups.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think at this stage a startup shouldn't spend too much energy agonizing over morphology. The form factor is a bit of a trap right now, because everyone is arguing about humanoid versus wheeled base versus dual-arm, and in my view that's not where the real bottleneck is. The bottleneck is the brain, not the body.

The way I think about it is that the body is the interface between the model and the physical world, and the model today is still too weak to make full use of any body, no matter how elegant it is. So if you build a very sophisticated humanoid with dexterous hands and legs, you've bought yourself a lot of hardware complexity, cost, and reliability problems, and your model can't yet exploit most of those degrees of freedom. You end up spending a year on hardware before you can even collect clean data.

So my advice would be: pick the simplest morphology that lets you get real data and real tasks going, and that your model can actually drive end to end. For a lot of teams that means a wheeled base with one or two arms and a simple gripper. It's boring, but it's cheap, it's stable, you can build many of them, and that matters a lot because data scale is what moves the model. Ten boring robots collecting data every day beat one beautiful humanoid sitting in the lab being debugged.

There's a second reason too. I think morphology will converge over time, probably toward something humanoid, because the world is built for humans and because in the long run you want to share data across bodies. But a startup doesn't need to be the one who proves that convergence right now. What you need is a model and a data flywheel that transfers across bodies. If your perception, your representations, your action model are reasonably body-agnostic, then switching morphology later is a cost, but not a fatal one. If you tie everything to one specific body too early, you can't switch at all.

So I'd put it this way: treat morphology as a decision you can revisit every year, not a founding bet. Commit to the model, commit to the data, commit to a real use case, and let the body be whatever is cheapest to get there. The one exception is if you really have a specific application, say a factory or a warehouse, where a particular form clearly unlocks the task. Then yes, go specific. But if you're doing something general, keep it simple and keep it flexible.

r001.rationale: The response says the main bottleneck is “the brain, not the body” and that today’s model is too weak to make full use of any morphology.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the task, rather than the shape of the robot. What does the customer need done, in what environment, and what level of reliability makes it worth paying for? Morphology should follow from those answers.

For a startup, that means choosing the simplest form that can deliver a useful result. If a fixed arm can do the job, you may not need a mobile robot. If wheels work, you need a clear reason to add legs. Every additional degree of freedom adds challenges in control, hardware reliability, and cost.

Humanoid robots are attractive because so much of our environment is designed for people. But that advantage matters only if your target task actually requires it. I would prioritize getting a complete system working reliably for a customer, then use what you learn from deployment to decide how the morphology should evolve.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes customer tasks, reliability, and choosing a simple morphology. It does not identify insufficient intelligence as the primary bottleneck.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a robotics startup should start with the task it wants to solve, and let that determine the morphology. Where will the robot work? What does it need to manipulate? How much mobility does it actually need? Those questions should come before deciding whether it looks like a human.

Every additional degree of freedom adds cost and complexity—in control, reliability, maintenance, and data collection. If a fixed arm or a wheeled platform can deliver value, that can be a better starting point than a full humanoid. But if the task requires moving through spaces designed for people and working at different heights, a more humanlike form may make sense.

At this stage, I would prioritize a system that can reliably complete a useful task and generate feedback from real deployment. Keep the design flexible enough to evolve, but make the initial morphology serve a clear customer need.

r001.rationale: The response prioritizes task fit, cost, complexity, and reliable deployment; it does not identify insufficient intelligence as the primary bottleneck.
